tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# Kitty: shared trip costs — design
2	
3	Date: 2026-11-17
4	
5	## Intent
6	
7	A command-line tool for tracking shared costs on trips with friends, so at the
8	end everyone knows who owes whom. The owner is not a programmer; their friend
9	Sam will drive it from scripts and pull the data into a spreadsheet. So output
10	must be machine-readable (JSON, CSV) and mistakes must produce a clear message,
11	never a crash.
12	
13	## Goals
14	
15	- Run as `python3 -m kitty <command>` from the folder, with the stock macOS
16	  Python (3.9.6). Standard library only, nothing to install.
17	- Keep all data in `kitty.json` in the current working directory.
18	- Exact money arithmetic (`decimal.Decimal`), with fully specified rounding so
19	  every split adds up to the cent and results are reproducible.
20	
21	## Non-goals
22	
23	- Several kitties per folder, editing existing entries (remove and re-add
24	  instead), undo, fetching exchange rates online, any GUI.
25	
26	## Anti-goals (a failure even if it "works")
27	
28	- Guessing: an unknown name, a currency with no rate, or a bad amount must be
29	  refused, never silently fixed up.
30	- Shares that don't add up exactly to the expense's main-currency amount.
31	- Past numbers changing on their own (changing a rate or removing a member must
32	  never alter recorded expenses).
33	- A Python traceback shown to the user for any input mistake.
34	- Needing anything beyond the stock Python.
35	
36	## Approaches
37	
38	1. **Small package with separate modules, plus unit tests** — chosen. Command
39	   parsing, money/splitting, storage and reports in separate files, so Sam can
40	   find and change one part safely. Tests pin down every agreed rule.
41	2. **Single file** — quicker to glance at, but this many commands and rules
42	   make one long file that's harder to change safely. Not chosen.
43	3. **Database or third-party libraries** — ruled out: must be plain Python and
44	   `kitty.json`.
45	
46	The owner left the technical choice to us; option 1 is our call.
47	
48	## Commands (decided by the owner/Sam)
49	
50	- `init CUR` — new kitty with main currency CUR.
51	- `member add NAME`, `member remove NAME`, `member list`.
52	- `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION [--among A,B | --exact A=30,B=20 |
53	  --shares A=2,B=1 | --percent A=60,B=40] [--currency CUR] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]
54	  [--category CAT]` — prints the new expense's ID. Default split: equally among
55	  all members. Default date: today. Default category: `other`.
56	- `expense list`, `expense remove ID`.
57	- `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency CUR] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]`.
58	- `rate set CUR VALUE` — one CUR is worth VALUE of the main currency.
59	- `balances`, `settle`, `history NAME`, `report`, `export FILE`.
60	
61	## Output formats (decided by Sam)
62	
63	JSON on stdout. Money is a string with exactly two decimals, in the main
64	currency, except an expense's own `amount`. Examples:
65	
66	- `member list`: `["Alice", "Bob"]`
67	- `expense list`: `[{"id": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice",
68	  "description": "Dinner", "amount": "45.00", "currency": "USD",
69	  "base_amount": "41.40", "category": "food", "shares": {"Alice": "20.70",
70	  "Bob": "20.70"}}]`
71	- `balances`: `{"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "-20.70"}`
72	- `settle`: `[{"from": "Bob", "to": "Alice", "amount": "20.70"}]`
73	- `history Bob`: `[{"date": "2026-07-14", "description": "Dinner",
74	  "change": "-20.70", "balance": "-20.70"}]`
75	- `report`: `{"food": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}`
76	
77	`export FILE` writes CSV with columns, in this order: `id, date, payer,
78	description, amount, currency, category, base_amount`.
79	
80	Errors: a message saying what's wrong, and exit status 1.
81	
82	## Rules decided by the owner
83	
84	**Exchange rates.** Each expense and payment is converted at the rate in effect
85	when it was added, and that rate is stored with it. Changing a rate only
86	affects entries added afterwards. Using a currency with no rate set is refused
87	with a reason (e.g. `no rate set for USD; use: rate set USD <value>`). Setting a
88	rate for the main currency is refused. The main currency's rate is always 1.
89	
90	**Conversion rounding.** `base_amount = amount × rate`, rounded to the cent with
91	halves always going up (0.125 → 0.13), i.e. `ROUND_HALF_UP`.
92	
93	**Splitting.** The main-currency amount (`base_amount`) is what gets split.
94	Every person's exact part is rounded *down* to the cent; the leftover cents are
95	then handed out one each, in order:
96	- `--among`, `--shares`, `--percent`, `--exact`: the order the names were typed;
97	- default (everyone): the order members joined.
98	
99	Examples: 10.00 among Alice, Bob, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
100	`--shares A=1,B=2` on 10.00 → A 3.34, B 6.66.
101	
102	**`--exact`.** Amounts are in the expense's own currency and must add up to the
103	expense amount exactly, or it's refused. For the main-currency shares they act
104	as weights: each person's exact part of `base_amount` is
105	`base_amount × their_amount / amount`, then the same round-down-and-hand-out
106	rule applies. (In the main currency this reproduces the typed amounts exactly.)
107	
108	**`--percent`.** Must add up to exactly 100, or it's refused.
109	
110	**Removing members.** Refused, with a reason, if the person appears anywhere:
111	payer of an expense, has a share in one, or sender/receiver of a payment.
112	Removing someone who appears nowhere is fine.
113	
114	**Settle.** Repeatedly: the person who owes the most pays the person owed the
115	most, the amount being the smaller of the two; repeat until all are even.
116	Ties (equal amounts) are broken alphabetically, ignoring capitals. Payments are
117	listed in the order they're worked out. Empty list `[]` when everyone is even.
118	
119	## Builder's calls (made by us; owner may correct)
120	
121	**Balances.** For each member: total `base_amount` of expenses they paid,
122	minus their shares, plus payments they sent, minus payments they received.
123	Positive = owed money. Output lists all current members in join order,
124	including `"0.00"` (never `"-0.00"`).
125	
126	**History.** Entries the person appears in (as payer, sharer, sender or
127	receiver), sorted by date, then by the order they were added. Includes entries
128	whose change is 0.00 (e.g. paid only for themselves). `change` for an expense =
129	(base_amount if they paid) − (their share); for a payment = +base_amount for the
130	sender, −base_amount for the receiver. Payment description:
131	`"Payment to Bob"` / `"Payment from Alice"`. `balance` is the running total;
132	the last one equals their `balances` value. NAME must be a current member.
133	
134	**Report.** Categories sorted alphabetically; within each, people in join order,
135	only those with a share in that category. Payments don't count.
136	
137	**Expense list / export.** Sorted by ID. `shares` keys in split order (as
138	above). Export overwrites an existing file, UTF-8, header row included, money
139	with two decimals.
140	
141	**Success output.** `expense add` prints just the ID number (e.g. `1`). Other
142	commands that change data print nothing.
143	
144	**IDs.** Expense IDs start at 1 and are never reused, even after removal.
145	Payments have no user-visible ID (none is needed by any command).
146	
147	**Input validation** (all refusals exit 1 with `error: ...` on stderr):
148	- No `kitty.json` (any command except `init`): say so and suggest
149	  `python3 -m kitty init EUR`. `init` when `kitty.json` exists: refuse.
150	  Unreadable/corrupt `kitty.json`: refuse with a message.
151	- Currency codes: three letters, accepted in any case and stored uppercase.
152	- Amounts: positive, digits with up to two decimals (`45`, `45.5`, `45.50`);
153	  anything else (`abc`, `-5`, `0`, `1e3`, `12.345`) refused.
154	- Rates: positive decimal number, any number of decimals.
155	- `--shares` values: positive numbers; `--percent` values: positive numbers
156	  summing to 100; `--exact` values: positive amounts (two decimals max).

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
